title: a full boss battle from my rock-paper-scissors deck battler (wip)
author: Natural-Spirit-3481
selftext:
The original idea for Hail Mary: Blitz began during the COVID lockdowns. I created a physical card game from scratch and played it with my younger brother and sister. It used counters and had a fast pace, but its rules and setup were completely different from the card game Speed. At the time, I didn't even know Speed existed.

I later tried turning my card game into an RPG prototype. That version had no real story progression or memorable characters, and the gameplay never felt fluid or fun. It helped me experiment with the concept, but it was clear that the project needed a different direction.

About a year ago, my girlfriend introduced me to Speed. It is a fast-paced two-player card game where both players race to empty their hands and draw piles. Playing it made me realize that the urgency of Speed could work really well with the counters, strategy, and ideas from the game I had created during lockdown.

That combination became the foundation of Hail Mary: Blitz.

Around four months ago, I began developing the current digital version with the help of Codex/GPT. Since then, I have used roughly 9 billion tokens across programming, debugging, game design, balancing, writing, interface development, and experimentation.

Hail Mary: Blitz has grown into a fast-paced Rock, Paper, Scissors card game with different card tiers, pickups, deck variants, bosses, challenges, progression systems, and several ways to play.

Current features currently includes:

* Quickplay with ten difficulty levels and deck-based progression
* Multiple deck variants that change how matches are approached
* Bronze, Silver, Gold, and Holo cards
* Pickups that can modify cards, disrupt opponents, or change a match
* Arcade activities such as Reaction Table, Streak Table, Time Attack, Rush Drill, Combo Trials, and Accuracy Trial
* Challenge Mode with specialized objectives and rule modifiers
* Case Files featuring bosses, evidence, contracts, dialogue, and final-form battles
* Casino Floor Run, a longer run-based mode with tables, bosses, upgrades, side activities, and jackpot progression
* Animated low-poly characters that react to the player’s mouse
* Local player profiles, match history, records, statistics, and unlock progression
* The Hail Mary Herald, an in-game newspaper that reveals Midnight Keys, lore, clues, and the path toward completing the larger mystery
* Music, a retro presentation, and a casino-inspired visual identity, although I still need proper sound effects

Codex/GPT has been involved throughout the development process, but it has not been as simple as asking it to create an entire game. My process is extremely iterative.

I describe a feature, test the implementation, identify what is broken, and then work through the problem with Codex/GPT. Sometimes a fix works immediately. Other times it introduces a new layout issue, navigation bug, stale state, incorrect save value, or gameplay inconsistency somewhere else.

A large part of the work has involved carefully explaining the intended behavior. That includes how menus should transition, how cards should resolve, how progression should be saved, how bosses should behave, and what the player should experience after every action.

I also review the results constantly because Codex/GPT can produce working code that still does not feel right as a game. Something can technically function while still being awkward, unbalanced, confusing, or visually inconsistent.

The visual design has followed the same process. I have repeatedly adjusted spacing, typography, animation, readability, responsiveness, and hierarchy. Codex/GPT can help build an interface quickly, but deciding whether it feels polished, understandable, and consistent still requires a lot of human judgment.

The game is much larger than the project I originally imagined. SCOPE CREEP AHHHHHH.

It also still has plenty of bugs to fix. Systems can conflict with one another, UI state can become corrupted, and a feature that works in one mode may behave differently in another. With so many connected systems, every change needs to be tested across multiple paths.

Even with those difficulties, Codex/GPT allowed me to build something I would not have been able to create at this scale on my own. I started with a homemade game that I played with my siblings during lockdown. An unsuccessful RPG prototype and a card game introduced to me by my girlfriend eventually helped reshape it into something much faster and more focused.

Hail Mary: Blitz is still a work in progress, but seeing that original family card game evolve into a complete digital world has been sick.
